title: Homogenization in the critical case for an optimal control problem with dynamic boundary conditions on microscopic particles: the homogenized system and the limit adjoint problem (Theorem 5.1)
author: Jesus Ildefonso Diaz; Tatyana A. Shaposhnikova; Alexander V. Podolskiy
work: New cost terms through homogenization of an optimal control problem under dynamic boundary conditions on microscopic particles
source_version: Electronic Journal of Differential Equations 2026, No. 18, pp. 1--26; DOI 10.58997/ejde.2026.18; publisher version
difficulty_reason: The counted theorem is the paper's main homogenization result and its proof is the whole difficulty of the unit. After the setting, the adjoint problem, the a priori estimates and the non-local in time operators of Sections 2 to 4 are supplied as context, the proof must still build a multi-scale construction: it constructs the auxiliary functions solving the model boundary-value problems on the dilated cells (lines 1286--1293) and glues them into the global alternating test functions associated with the controlled and the uncontrolled particles (lines 1298--1313); it applies the surface-to-volume averaging convergence principle (lines 1361--1374) so that the boundary integrals over the particle boundaries of the critical case become volume terms carrying the two thresholds of the limit problem and the strange terms; it then runs four separate passages to the limit for the state equation (Steps A.1 to A.4, lines 1318--1601), where the surfaces of the two particle families must be tracked separately and the limits of the surface terms are identified through the three auxiliary non-local operators; it then repeats the analysis for the adjoint equation (Steps B.1 to B.3, lines 1616--1798), where the combination multiplying the limit adjoint state only collapses to the closed form of the limit operator after the second relation of Lemma 4.1 is used (lines 1657--1671); and it closes by upgrading the subsequence convergences to the whole sequences through the well-posedness of the limit problem (lines 1817--1819). The critical scaling of the radius is exactly what makes the strange terms appear simultaneously in the state equation, in the adjoint equation and in the cost functional, and there is no textbook or qualifying-exam counterpart: each step is a source-local device of this paper. The unit is therefore graded H3 rather than H2.
